prompt: Which syntax difference is correct?
options: IPv6 routes use dotted-decimal subnet masks.
IPv4 static routes must always use link-local next hops.
IPv6 uses prefix/length and scopes link-local next hops by interface.
IPv6 route commands select a source rather than a destination.
explanation: IPv6 uses slash prefix notation. The link-local scope rule is an additional constraint on its next-hop form.

whyWrong.0: Dotted subnet masks are the IPv4 form here.
whyWrong.1: IPv4 statics do not have the IPv6 link-local scope rule.
whyWrong.3: The route identifies destination reachability; it does not generally choose the packet source.

prompt: In S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [1/0], what are the bracketed numbers?
options: Administrative distance 1 and metric 0
Metric 1 and administrative distance 0
One route advertisement and zero errors
One next-hop router and zero alternate paths
explanation: IOS displays [administrative distance/metric]. These values do not count traffic events or alternate routes.

whyWrong.2: The fields are not packet or advertisement counters.
whyWrong.3: Next-hop and path counts are not encoded in this pair.

prompt: Which statement correctly reads the installed static entry?
options: The remote /64 uses fe80::2 on Gi0/0 with distance 1.
The /64 has a hop count of 1 and a loss count of 0.
The route describes R1's own local /128 address.
The route applies only to a host whose suffix is ::2.
explanation: The destination prefix is 2001:db8:20::/64; the bracketed values are distance and metric. The interface scopes the link-local next hop.

whyWrong.1: The brackets are not hop count and loss count.
whyWrong.2: The S /64 is a remote static network route, not an L /128.
whyWrong.3: fe80::2 is the next hop, not the destination prefix's host identifier.

prompt: Which global command enables inter-interface IPv6 forwarding on the basic IOS router?
options: ipv6 enable
ipv6 unicast-routing
ip routing
ipv6 address autoconfig
explanation: ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 router forwarding. Interfaces also need appropriate addressing and usable links.

whyWrong.0: ipv6 enable is an interface command for IPv6 processing/link-local operation.
whyWrong.2: ip routing controls IPv4 forwarding.
whyWrong.3: Autoconfig is an interface address-assignment instruction, not this global forwarding setting.

prompt: An IOS router has active IPv6-addressed interfaces but no ipv6 unicast-routing. In this basic unfiltered setup, which TWO behaviors are expected?
options: It can answer a directly attached host pinging its own interface address.
It forwards packets between its IPv6 interfaces normally.
It does not provide the required inter-interface IPv6 forwarding.
Its interface IPv6 addresses must immediately be erased.
explanation: The router can function as an IPv6 endpoint without being enabled to forward IPv6 traffic between interfaces.

whyWrong.1: That forwarding requires the global IPv6 routing setting in this setup.
whyWrong.3: Disabling forwarding does not erase assigned interface addresses.

prompt: R1 is configured with a distance-1 primary and distance-5 backup. What does this installed entry establish?
options: The primary cable is certainly unplugged.
The backup has exactly five intermediate hops.
The backup is selected; the cause needs more evidence.
The backup is only configured and cannot forward traffic.
explanation: The table shows the selected backup. The absence of the primary alone does not distinguish physical failure from other eligibility or configuration causes.

whyWrong.0: A table entry does not uniquely prove a cable fault.
whyWrong.3: This is the installed table, so the route is selected; neighbor and end-to-end checks still matter.

prompt: Neighbor fe80::2 is reachable on R1 Gi0/0. Which command routes the remote 2001:db8:20::/64 through that neighbor?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ip route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ipv6 route fe80::2/128 gigabitethernet0/0 2001:db8:20::
explanation: The fully specified IPv6 command supplies the destination prefix, local interface and link-local next hop.

whyWrong.0: A link-local next hop needs an interface.
whyWrong.2: ip route is the IPv4 command family.
whyWrong.3: This changes the destination into the neighbor's own link-local address instead of the remote LAN.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 fe80::2
The command is rejected; exact error text varies by image.

prompt: Why does the shown command lack required information?
options: The command must include the source LAN prefix before its destination prefix.
A link-local next hop can never carry routed traffic.
The link-local next hop needs its exit interface.
The neighbor hardware address must be appended to the route.
explanation: A link-local address is meaningful on a particular link, so the IOS route must name that link's interface.

whyWrong.0: An ordinary destination static route does not require a source-prefix field.
whyWrong.1: Link-local next hops are valid when scoped to the correct interface.
whyWrong.3: The command needs IPv6 next-hop scope; ND supplies its Ethernet binding.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Primary: R1 Gi0/0 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/0 fe80::2
Backup: R1 Gi0/1 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/1 fe80::3
Remote LAN behind R2: 2001:db8:20::/64

prompt: R1 must route the remote LAN through R2 on the primary link. Which choice uses the correct scoped link-local next hop?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::1
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
explanation: R2's primary link-local address is fe80::2, reachable through R1 Gi0/0.

whyWrong.0: fe80::1 is R1's own local address in this plan.
whyWrong.1: fe80::2 is not the peer on the backup link.
whyWrong.2: The link-local next hop lacks an interface.

prompt: Which command adds an IPv6 default using the resolvable non-link-local next hop 2001:db8:12::2?
explanation: ::/0 matches all IPv6 addresses and provides the default when no longer installed prefix matches.

whyWrong.0: ::/128 identifies one special address, not all destinations.
whyWrong.1: An IPv4 dotted destination is not the IPv6 default syntax.
whyWrong.2: Use ipv6 route for this address family.

prompt: A working /64 route uses Gi0/0. Only 2001:db8:20::12 should use usable backup neighbor fe80::3 on Gi0/1. Which addition achieves that?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
explanation: A /128 matches only that host, leaving other /64 addresses on their existing network route.

whyWrong.0: Another /64 affects the whole network candidate, not just one host.
whyWrong.2: A default cannot override the existing /64 for that host.
whyWrong.3: A host address with /64 does not describe the intended single-address route.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::3 5

prompt: Both links and their neighbors are usable. Which TWO statements follow from the configured routes?
options: The primary is preferred because its ordinary distance is 1.
The distance-5 route forwards half the traffic while the primary is installed.
The backup can become selected if the preferred route is withdrawn.
Distance 5 means the backup traverses five routers.
explanation: These are candidates for the same /64. Lower distance selects the primary; the backup can be selected after withdrawal if its path remains usable.

whyWrong.1: The unequal distances implement standby rather than equal-cost multipath.
whyWrong.3: The final 5 is administrative distance, not a hop count.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
::/0 via Gi0/0, distance 1
2001:db8:20::/64 via Gi0/1, distance 1
2001:db8:20::12/128 via Gi0/2, distance 200

prompt: All displayed routes are installed. Which interface handles destination 2001:db8:20::12?
options: Gi0/2, because the /128 is the longest match
Gi0/1, because its distance is less than 200
Gi0/0, because a default takes priority
All three, because the address matches all three
explanation: The /128 matches the single destination more specifically than /64 or /0. Different installed prefix lengths are not ranked by distance during forwarding.

whyWrong.1: The lower distance of a different prefix does not override the /128.
whyWrong.2: A default is the least specific match.
whyWrong.3: Overlapping prefixes do not form equal-cost paths to the same prefix.

prompt: A repeated test cannot resolve fe80::2 on Gi0/1. Another cache entry shows fe80::2 on Gi0/0. What should you check?
options: Use the Gi0/0 binding automatically for all interfaces.
Verify whether the intended peer actually owns fe80::2 on the Gi0/1 link.
Assume the repeated address proves global routing is disabled.
Delete all IPv6 routes because a neighbor state is not REACH.
explanation: Link-local neighbor identity includes its link. A binding on Gi0/0 does not establish a valid next hop on Gi0/1.

whyWrong.0: Cross-link reuse ignores scope and cannot supply the required neighbor.
whyWrong.2: The evidence concerns one address/interface binding, not the global forwarding setting.
whyWrong.3: Non-REACH states have different meanings; inspect the targeted fault rather than deleting all routes.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
!
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0
Remote PC 2001:db8:20::12 is behind R2, not on this transit link.

prompt: R2 owns the remote LAN, but no proxy ND is configured. Why is this Ethernet interface-only route inappropriate for reaching a host behind R2?
options: It attempts discovery for the remote host on the transit link.
It causes R1 to ask ARP for the remote IPv6 host.
The interface-only form automatically discovers the correct remote router through RA.
The Ethernet interface supplies the remote PC MAC without Neighbor Discovery.
explanation: With no explicit next hop, the route makes remote destinations appear on-link. The remote PC does not hear neighbor discovery on the transit segment.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, not ARP.
whyWrong.2: An interface-only route does not identify that adjacent next hop.
whyWrong.3: Ethernet delivery still requires a usable neighbor mapping.

prompt: Which neighbor-cache observation requires additional investigation rather than proving success or failure by its label alone?
options: STALE lacks recent confirmation; test the intended neighbor and inspect the resulting state and traffic.
An empty cache proves the configured peer is absent from the link.
One INCOMPLETE entry proves the entire remote LAN is unreachable permanently.
STALE means the address is duplicated and must be reassigned.
explanation: Neighbor states describe the local resolution/reachability process. Combine them with the intended interface, traffic and repeated observations.

whyWrong.1: The cache contains discovered bindings, not a complete device inventory.
whyWrong.2: Resolution can be in progress; persistent failure and the correct link/address must be checked.
whyWrong.3: DAD evidence, not the STALE reachability state, identifies duplicates.

prompt: Which two observations make these repeated link-local next hops unambiguous? Choose two.
options: Both routes use the same address text, so they must point to one physical router.
Neighbor entries can be combined without keeping their interface field.
The router must replace one link-local address with a global address.
Each route supplies its own local exit interface.
FE80::2 is verified on the adjacent peer interface of each separate link.
explanation: Two separate links may each contain FE80::2. The route and neighbor cache must preserve the interface/address pair.

whyWrong.0: Repeated link-local text does not identify a global device.
whyWrong.1: Discarding the interface loses the necessary link-local scope.
whyWrong.2: The interface scopes the next hop, so replacement is not required.

exhibit.title: Repeated link-local next hops (exercise)
exhibit.text:
ipv6 route 2001:db8:21:1::/64 Gi0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:21:2::/64 Gi0/1 FE80::2
Gi0/0 and Gi0/1 connect to different routed links.

prompt: Which installed route carries a packet to 2001:db8:44:ab3d::8?
options: 2001:db8:44:ab30::/61 through FE80::4 on Gi0/2
2001:db8:44:ab38::/61 through FE80::3 on Gi0/1
2001:db8:44:ab30::/60 through FE80::2 on Gi0/0
::/0 through FE80::5 on Gi0/3
explanation: The fourth group ab3d is inside ab38 through ab3f. Match prefix bits before comparing candidate distances for the same prefix.

whyWrong.0: That /61 covers ab30 through ab37, not ab3d.
whyWrong.2: The /60 matches, but the /61 matches more retained bits.
whyWrong.3: A default loses to a longer installed match.

prompt: After the exact temporary /128 is removed, which route matches the same destination?
options: The installed /64 network route.
No route, because deleting a host route also deletes its containing network route.
The default, because it has lower distance than the /64.
A local L route, because every deleted static becomes local.
explanation: The next longest installed match is the /64. Configuration cleanup should name the exact temporary route so the baseline remains intact.

whyWrong.1: Removing one exact configured static does not remove a separate /64.
whyWrong.2: The /64 is a longer destination match than /0.
whyWrong.3: Local routes represent addresses owned by this router, not deleted remote statics.

exhibit.title: Routes before exact cleanup (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Before cleanup:
S 2001:db8:24::44/128 [50/0] via FE80::3, Gi0/1
S 2001:db8:24::/64 [20/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S ::/0 [1/0] via FE80::4, Gi0/2
Only the /128 configuration is removed.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:10::11 behind R1
PC-B: 2001:db8:20::12 behind R2
Complete relevant R2 unicast routes; no default:
C 2001:DB8:12::/64, Gi0/0
L 2001:DB8:12::2/128, Gi0/0
C 2001:DB8:20::/64, Gi0/2
L 2001:DB8:20::1/128, Gi0/2

prompt: Both hosts have correct local gateways and all links work. R1 has a route to PC-B's LAN. Which missing route explains why replies to PC-A cannot return through R2?
options: An R1 route to R2's already connected transit prefix
An R2 host route to its own LAN address
An R2 route to LAN 20 through its own local interface address
An R2 route covering 2001:db8:10::/64 through R1
explanation: The reply destination is PC-A in 2001:db8:10::/64. R2's supplied complete table lacks that prefix or a covering default.

whyWrong.0: R1's connected transit is not the missing reverse destination.
whyWrong.1: R2 already owns its local LAN address.
whyWrong.2: LAN 20 is already local to R2 and does not cover the reply destination in LAN 10.

prompt: Why does the intended standby path already carry traffic for 2001:db8:18::25?
options: The host route is used only after Neighbor Discovery on the /64 fails.
The /64 primary must have been removed because the /128 appears.
All distance-50 statics automatically override distance-1 statics.
The /128 is more specific; distance 50 does not make it a standby for the /64.
explanation: Floating candidates must cover the same intended prefix. A host route is independently eligible and wins the longest-match lookup for that host.

whyWrong.0: The /128 wins at route selection before a /64 neighbor failure is relevant.
whyWrong.1: Different prefix lengths can coexist in the installed table.
whyWrong.2: Lower distance is preferred between usable candidates for the same prefix.

exhibit.title: Network and host route overlap (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Both interfaces are up and both next hops resolve.
S 2001:db8:18::/64 [1/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S 2001:db8:18::25/128 [50/0] via FE80::3, Gi0/1

prompt: Which missing information should be checked before assuming this configured static can install?
options: A usable route resolving 2001:db8:120::2 without circular dependence.
A matching IPv4 static route to the same last two address groups.
A host route to every address inside the destination /64.
A MAC address written directly into the ipv6 route command.
explanation: The global next-hop-only form relies on recursive resolution. The connected /64 shown is a different prefix from the configured next hop.

whyWrong.1: IPv4 routes do not resolve an IPv6 next hop.
whyWrong.2: A network route can cover the destination LAN.
whyWrong.3: Static route configuration uses an IPv6 next hop; ND resolves the Ethernet neighbor later.

exhibit.title: Recursive next-hop reachability (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Configured: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 2001:db8:120::2
Only connected transit prefix: 2001:db8:12::/64
No other route to 2001:db8:120::2 and no default.
The desired remote /64 is absent from the installed table.

prompt: What is the missing part of the redundant routing design?
options: A higher distance on R1 primary so that it never returns.
A second copy of R1 backup route with the same values.
A default gateway on R1 pointing at PC-A.
A usable backup return route on R2 to PC-A LAN.
explanation: The backup must work in both directions for the tested sources. R1 route failover alone does not establish the reply path.

whyWrong.0: This does not supply R2 missing reverse route.
whyWrong.1: R1 already has the outbound backup; copying it does not alter R2 return path.
whyWrong.2: PC-A is an endpoint, not the next-hop router for the remote network.

exhibit.title: Forward and return routes after failure (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Primary directly cabled link fails; backup link and both LANs remain up.
R1 now installs LAN-B /64 via the backup.
R2 lost its only route to LAN-A /64; it has no default.
Both PCs retain their correct on-link gateways.
PC-A to PC-B still fails.

prompt: Which conclusion about this failed remote ping is justified?
options: The backup must install whenever any destination stops replying.
An ordinary static route can remain selected while a failure beyond its usable next hop breaks delivery.
A reachable next hop proves the remote LAN and its return route work.
Reducing both route distances to 1 creates reliable failure detection.
explanation: Route installation and successful delivery are different. Inspect downstream and reverse paths before treating the configured distance as a health monitor.

whyWrong.0: An ordinary static route does not monitor every end-to-end destination.
whyWrong.2: Local next-hop reachability does not establish downstream or return reachability.
whyWrong.3: That changes route preference or multipath behavior, not end-to-end health detection.

exhibit.title: Remote failure with an installed primary (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Primary and backup statics cover the same /64 at distances 1 and 20.
Primary exit interface is up; its connected next hop still answers.
The installed route remains the primary.
A remote failure beyond that neighbor prevents replies; no tracking is configured.

prompt: Which missing return prefix explains why the endpoint test fails while the explicitly sourced router test succeeds?
options: R2 needs a route covering 2001:db8:12::1, the connected transit source.
R2 needs a route covering 2001:db8:10::11, the client source.
PC-A should use R2 remote-LAN address as an on-link gateway.
R1 needs another route to 2001:db8:20::/64, the already covered destination.
explanation: The tests differ in source address. A reply to R1 transit address uses R2 connected route; a reply to PC-A requires the missing client-LAN route.

whyWrong.0: R2 already reaches that transit source through its connected prefix.
whyWrong.2: That remote address is not on PC-A local link.
whyWrong.3: The supplied outbound route already covers the destination.

exhibit.title: Two ping sources and the return table (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1: LAN 2001:db8:10::/64; transit 2001:db8:12::1/64
R2: transit 2001:db8:12::2/64; LAN 2001:db8:20::/64
R1 has a route to LAN 20. R2 has only those two connected prefixes.
R1 ping to LAN-20 host with explicit source 2001:db8:12::1 succeeds.
PC-A 2001:db8:10::11 uses its correct local R1 gateway; the same destination test fails.

prompt: What happens while the selected host route remains installed and its next hop cannot be resolved?
options: Delivery through that host route fails; the router does not simply retry the less-specific /64 as a substitute.
The default route automatically replaces the /128 for that packet.
The router automatically forwards the same packet using the /64 because it has lower distance.
The neighbor failure proves that the destination host itself is powered off.
explanation: Correct syntax and installation do not prove next-hop delivery. Repair the verified scope/address error or remove the incorrect host route after diagnosis.

whyWrong.1: A default is less specific than both supplied routes.
whyWrong.2: Longest matching installed prefix is selected first; failed ND does not make a less-specific route the normal fallback.
whyWrong.3: It concerns the next hop on the transit link, not necessarily the remote host.

exhibit.title: Selected host route and unresolved neighbor (exercise)
exhibit.text:
S 2001:db8:23::/64 [1/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S 2001:db8:23::50/128 [200/0] via FE80::9, Gi0/1
After repeated traffic, FE80::9 cannot resolve on Gi0/1.
The /128 remains installed; the /64 path is otherwise healthy.
